newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives running out of firms to privatise.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives running out of firms to privatise.

text.p: Privatisation is one of the magic ingredients that has kept Britain's Conservative Party in office since it swept to power in 1979. But the magic potion is running out.
After an 18-year, 65 billion pound state sell-off, the Conservatives are running short of companies to privatise.

"Privatisation has gone from the dream of a few Conservative visionaries to the big idea which is transforming decaying public sector industries in almost every country in the world," proclaimed the party's manifesto for the May 1 election, launched on Wednesday.
"Britain has led the way with this new industrial revolution: we can be proud of what we achieved."

The Conservatives say the privatisation experiment which former prime minister Margaret Thatcher applied to Britain has revitalised economies from Africa to the former communist countries of Eastern Europe.

Their manifesto pledged to continue the privatisation drive in Britain. "Privatisation works," it said. "We will therefore continue to pass government activities into private ownership where this can bring benefits to consumers and taxpayers."

But privatisation pledges in the manifesto are limited. The party repeated its commitment to privatise London's cash-strapped underground rail network and re-invest the proceeds to improve transport in Britain.

It pledged to sell off the Parcelforce arm of Britain's national Post Office, and to consider "different forms of privatisation" for the Royal Mail postal service. Finally, it restated a pledge to sell off the air traffic control network.

Analysts say privatisation of all three arms of the Post office -- Parcelforce, the Royal Mail and Post Office Counters -- could raise around two billion pounds. London's underground sytem could also raise up to two billion, according to estimates.

But such sell-offs are small fare compared with the 14.2 billion pounds earned by the privatisation of British Telecommunications Plc in 1984 or the 10.35 billion raised from the sale of Britain's electricity companies in 1990.
The golden age of big British privatisations is over, analysts say. The Conservatives' cupboard is increasingly bare, and most of the prime targets for privatisation have already been sold.

Conservative hopes that their new privatisation pledges will prove vote-spinners which will cut the party's deficit in opinion polls are also likely to be disappointed, analysts say. Selling the Post Office and London Underground is unlikely to attract widespread popularity.
An earlier attempt to privatise the Post Office was shelved in 1994 when dissenters within the Conservative Party rebelled over the proposal.
And at a news conference on Wednesday, Prime Minister John Major himself admitted that selling the London Underground might not win votes.
"It may not be a vote winner," Major said. "We are taking actions that are in the interests of the country, even if they may not necessarily be a short-term vote winner."

Supporters of privatisation say companies like British Telecom and British Petroleum Plc have been transformed into world-beaters after being sold, and the breadth of share ownership in Britain has been expanded.
Even the left-of-centre Labour Party, which is widely forecast to win on May 1, has largely abandoned its hostility to the idea.

Labour says it would not privatise the underground but it has dropped pledges to renationalise privatised companies. Even the controversial sale of rail network operator Railtrack Plc is unlikely to be reversed under Labour.

But the days when the Conservatives could count on privatisation as an ideological rallying-cry and vote winner are over, analysts say. Unless the party is prepared to adopt ever more radical sell-off proposals, the privatisation bandwagon is unlikely to have much further to roll in Britain. ($ = 0.606 British Pounds)
